---
title: "Career"
subtitle: "From a junior Wimbledon champion in 1998 to a farewell at the 2022 Laver Cup"
---

## Timeline

| Year | Milestone |
|------|-----------|
| 1998 | Wins the Wimbledon boys' singles title; turns professional. |
| 2001 | Ends Pete Sampras's 31-match Wimbledon win streak in the fourth round. |
| 2003 | Wins his first Grand Slam title at Wimbledon. |
| 2004 | Wins three majors in a season and reaches No. 1 for the first time (2 February 2004). |
| 2006 | Goes 92–5 on the season, reaching all four major finals. |
| 2009 | Completes the Career Grand Slam by winning the French Open; breaks Sampras's record of 14 majors at Wimbledon. |
| 2012 | Wins a seventh Wimbledon title and returns to No. 1, extending his record for weeks at the top. |
| 2017 | Wins the Australian Open and Wimbledon at age 35 after a six-month injury layoff. |
| 2018 | Defends the Australian Open for a 20th and final major title; briefly returns to No. 1 at age 36, the oldest man to hold the ranking. |
| 2019 | Loses a five-set Wimbledon final to Novak Djokovic after holding two championship points. |
| 2021 | Plays his final competitive singles matches at Wimbledon. |
| 2022 | Retires at the Laver Cup in London, playing a farewell doubles match alongside Rafael Nadal. |

## Weeks at World No. 1

Federer first reached No. 1 on 2 February 2004 and held the position for 237
consecutive weeks through 17 August 2008 — a record that still stands. He
reclaimed the top ranking several times, most improbably in 2018 at age 36. His
total of 310 weeks at No. 1 was a record until surpassed by Novak Djokovic.

| Ranking record | Detail |
|----------------|--------|
| Total weeks at No. 1 | 310 |
| Consecutive weeks at No. 1 | 237 (record) |
| Year-end No. 1 finishes | 5 (2004–2007, 2009) |
| Years in the top 10 | 14 consecutive (2002–2016), then 2017–2020 |

## Surface strengths

Federer won titles on every surface but built his legend on fast courts. He was
especially dominant on grass, where he won 8 Wimbledon titles and 10 Halle
titles, and on indoor hard courts, where he won his home event in Basel 10 times.
His lone French Open title in 2009 completed the Career Grand Slam and came the
year Rafael Nadal was upset before the final.

## Playing style

- **One-handed backhand** — a signature shot, refined late in his career into an
  aggressive weapon after coaching work with Ivan Ljubičić.
- **Serve** — not the fastest on tour, but among the most accurate and
  disguised, letting him hold serve cheaply for two decades.
- **Movement** — widely praised footwork that kept points short and reduced wear
  on his body, contributing to his longevity.
- **SABR** — the "Sneak Attack By Roger," a chip-charge return off second serves
  he introduced in 2015.
